source.title: The Theoretical Expressiveness of Maxpooling
source.authors: Kyle Matoba; Nikolaos Dimitriadis; François Fleuret

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation affecting the reported experiments.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses generalizability, but its experiments compare max-pooling and convolutional variants on clean accuracy and adversarial robustness. It does not measure training-to-test gaps, random-label memorization, or convolutional versus fully connected test error as V3 specifies.
record.gate_note: Theoretical analysis concerns approximating max functions, not the claim's training-to-test generalization gap. The experiments report clean and adversarial accuracy for max-pooling and convolutional CNN variants; those comparisons do not test any listed version. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study compares max-pooling CNNs with CNNs using convolutional replacements and analyzes approximation of the max function. It does not compare convolutional with fully connected networks as V3 requires, or test any other listed version. Held-out accuracy is relevant evidence in principle; the architectural comparison, rather than the absence of training-to-test gaps, excludes these results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the empirical conclusions: the authors consider pooling replaceable when classification accuracy alone is the goal, while suggesting benefits for robustness and generalizability. The larger convolutional ResNet replacement matches FGSM robust accuracy at more than twice the parameter count. Their main contribution is theoretical approximation analysis within restricted function classes; generalizability benefits are suggested rather than established for any listed version.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments train CNN and ResNet variants with max-pooling or convolutional replacements and evaluate clean and FGSM robust accuracy; they do not use the original claim's label-memorization or train-test-gap methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, replacement type, perturbation magnitude, and model parameter count vary; robust accuracy changes across perturbation magnitudes.

fits_no_version.finding: Max-pooling variants have higher mean clean accuracy than their convolutional replacements in all three experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing max pooling with learned convolutional operations can reduce held-out accuracy in the tested MNIST and CIFAR-10 CNNs.

fits_no_version.finding: FGSM comparisons generally favor max pooling over the smaller convolutional replacements; the larger ResNet replacement achieves comparable robust accuracy with more than twice the parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Max pooling can improve FGSM robustness relative to convolutional replacements at lower parameter cost in the tested architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: The theoretical analysis bounds max-function approximation error and computational requirements for restricted classes of subpool-max approximations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Approximating max pooling within the analyzed function classes entails an approximation-error versus computational-complexity tradeoff.

record.problems: The experiments report test accuracy but no training accuracy or train-test gap. Robust-accuracy comparisons use FGSM, and the paper notes that its LeNet variants are not state of the art.
record.rows_left_out: Adversarial-accuracy values across perturbation magnitudes in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3, 5 and 6 are not extracted: adversarial robustness is outside the claim's specified versions and is discussed as a separate property. Theoretical approximation-error results concern the max function, not model generalization.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance under the same training recipe.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out error, local-connectivity contributions, learned sparse connections, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization and dependence on tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty. Ghost Batch Normalization is used without a relevant batch-size comparison.
Dropout effects and dependence on training-set size, dropout strength, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures. Input adversarial perturbations do not measure this.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: All nine rows retain their reported table values and links to none. Their states indicate inability to determine a listed version, not absence of the observed clean-accuracy differences. Robustness and theoretical results were already declared in rows_left_out and require no missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error, and the specified local-connectivity comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and their tuning or training conditions.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout’s effect on held-out error and its interaction with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the training-to-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
